newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: EU parliamentarian says Slovaks control own destiny.
newsitem.headline: EU parliamentarian says Slovaks control own destiny.

text.p: A European parliamentarian warned Slovakia on Wednesday to stop foot-dragging in democratic reforms towards EU integration saying the fate of union membership lay in the government's hands.

"It is exclusively in the hands of the political leadership of this country whether it will become a European Union member at the same time as the Czech Republic or Hungary," Herbert Bosch, co-chairman of a joint EU-Slovak Parliamentary Committee, told journalists in Bratislava.
"The movement (towards the EU) is in the right direction, but Slovakia must get into higher gear," Bosch said at the end of a three-day committee session which meets twice a year.
But Bosch warned Slovakia against blamimg the EU for its possible failure to be in the first ranks of contenders for membership.
In the last two years Slovakia has come under fire from the EU and the United States for failing to fully implement democratic reforms.
But Slovak officials have dismissed such allegations, blaming a lack of information on the side of the critics who, it says, listen only to the country's political opposition.

The latest wave of criticism came last week from U.S. ambasssador to Slovakia Ralph Johnson and EU representative in Bratislava Georgios Zavvos, both of whom chided Slovakia for its foot-dragging towards democratic reforms.
"There is no discrimination of Slovakia in any form," Bosch said. "Movement toward the EU is the Slovak government's job."

The joint committee discussed a range of issues related to Slovakia's EU integration ambitions and noted some progress in the recent past such as the revival of a dialogue between the ruling coalition of premier Vladimir Meciar and the opposition.
Bosch, who is also chairman of the European Parliament's budget committee, said he was disapointed with Slovakia's tepid interest in making use of EU financial assistance through its Phare programme.
"If somebody says 'yes' to the EU, they must also say 'yes' to money from Phare, because anything else would be contradictory," he said.

According to the Phare agreement with the EU, Slovakia was entitled to spend 40 million ECU annually from 1995 to 1999 on projects to improve the infrastructure and develop the private economic sector.
But the annual tranche was cut this year by the Phare management to 26 million ECU, because Slovakia has failed to make full use of the amount offered.
The Slovak government has justified its indifference to the Phare project by citing "unacceptable conditions" demanded by the EU such as control over the way the money is spent.
